Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure
  - Soreness and cracking dry skin of the hands, predominantly the palms, present for about 3–4 months.
  - Occupational exposure: hotel housekeeping; inconsistent glove use while cleaning; recently changed job ~4 months ago.
- Symptom timeline and progression
  - Gradual onset over several months; recently worsened with pain limiting ability to work; has caused three days of work absence.
- ENT symptoms
  - None reported (no throat, airway, nasal, or ear symptoms).
- Past medical history and treatments
  - Diabetes mellitus type 2 on metformin.
  - No prior eczema/dermatitis diagnosed; no known skin problems in past.
  - Prior treatments for this condition: OTC moisturizers (E45) and an antihistamine without relief.
- Allergies and current medications
  - Allergies: not documented as present.
  - Medications: Metformin (dose/frequency not documented).
- Social/context
  - Works as a housekeeper in a hotel; gloves not consistently worn; no smoking; drinks a couple of pints of alcohol per week.
  - No other acute social considerations noted.

Objective:
- Observable findings
  - Palms described as very cracked, dry, and itchy with bleeding only when scratched.
  - No systemic symptoms or fever reported.
- Airway/breathing
  - Not applicable; no airway symptoms.
- Mental status
  - Not described.
- Vital signs
  - Not recorded.
- Additional observations
  - No other body regions described as involved beyond milder dryness on legs; no swelling of face/neck.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression
  - Hand dermatitis/eczema, with a high likelihood of irritant contact dermatitis given occupational exposure to cleaning products and intermittent glove use; palm-predominant involvement with cracking and itch.
- Brief evidence summary (from transcript)
  - Onset over months with worsening pain affecting work; correlation with cleaning duties and glove use; improvement not achieved with basic emollients/antihistamines.
- DDx reference (top 3 aligned with transcript)
  - Irritant contact dermatitis (high likelihood)
    - Rationale: occupational exposure to cleaning products, inconsistent gloves, palmar fissuring and pruritus; chronic course.
    - Opposing evidence: no specific irritant identified or patch-testing data yet.
  - Allergic contact dermatitis (possible)
    - Rationale: exposure to cleaning agents could trigger sensitization; pruritus and fissuring fit dermatitis spectrum.
    - Opposing evidence: no identified allergen or patch-test result yet.
  - Hand dermatitis/eczema (including possible atopic component)
    - Rationale: chronic dry, itchy hands with fissures compatible with dermatitis/eczema.
    - Opposing evidence: no personal atopy history documented.
- Conflict note
  - No explicit conflicts between transcript and DDx; DDx offers useful context but aligns with transcript findings. Conflict noted: none.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised
  - Implement preventive measures: wear gloves during cleaning at all times.
  - Initiate treatment for inflammation and dryness:
    - Topical corticosteroid cream to reduce inflammation.
    - Stronger emollients/occlusives to improve moisture and barrier repair (applied regularly, multiple times daily for 2 weeks).
  - Follow-up plan: re-evaluate in 1–2 weeks; sooner if symptoms worsen or spread.
- Specific patient/caregiver instructions
  - Use gloves consistently during cleaning; avoid irritants when possible; moisturize hands several times daily.
  - Apply topical steroid as directed and reapply emollients after washing hands and as needed.
  - Return sooner if swelling, redness, blistering, increased pain, or new symptoms develop (e.g., spreading dermatitis).
- Escalation criteria / red flags
  - Worsening pain or swelling; spreading dermatitis; signs of infection (fever, purulent discharge); inability to use hands due to pain.
- Follow-up and referrals
  - Consider dermatology/allergy referral if persistent or if patch testing is pursued to identify specific allergens.
  - Counseling on occupational prevention and skin protection emphasized.
- DDx-informed recommendations
  - Patch testing considered if allergic dermatitis suspected or if no improvement with initial management.

COVID-19 vaccine suitability
- Not discussed/not applicable.

Document quality (clinical element checks):
- Missing elements likely expected in an acute ENT/allergy presentation
  - Specific allergen exposure details (if allergic dermatitis suspected) and patch-test planning.
  - Exact medication doses, routes, and frequencies for current prescriptions (metformin dose/frequency not documented).
  - Objective vitals and formal ENT exam findings (not recorded in transcript).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx
  - None identified; DDx supports the transcript’s likely irritant/contact dermatitis.
- Transcript quality notes
  - Overall coherent; lacks formal vitals and detailed physical exam documentation; dermatologic specifics (e.g., lesion morphology beyond fissures) are limited.

Note: All content remains faithful to the transcript and the structured DDx, with the transcript prioritized when discrepancies arise.
